summary:
Liberia criminalises consensual same-sex conduct between adults. The statute carries up to one year of imprisonment and applies to both sexes. It is a domestically originated law: Liberia was not colonised, so no foreign penal code was imposed on this point.

The existing statute is not the only legal exposure. In the summer of 2024, Representative Johnson N. Williams began seeking fellow lawmakers' support for a harsh anti-homosexuality bill, and related proposals filed alongside it would imprison children as young as 10 years old for gay sex. The bill had not been enacted as of October 2024.

Legislative hostility has a longer record. In 2012, new legislation was proposed that would have lengthened jail time for homosexuality, at a moment when anti-gay sentiment was rising after a foreign government announced plans to promote LGBT rights overseas. In the same period, a group distributed fliers targeting supporters of gay rights.

Senior political leadership has publicly defended the criminal law. In March 2012, President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, defended the laws criminalising homosexuality in a joint interview in Monrovia; her remarks drew international comment, while her interview partner declined to address the question.

Violence against gender-variant people is documented, including mob attacks. There is no legal mechanism for gender recognition: a trans visitor has no route to have their gender marker changed or recognised in Liberian documents.

The United Nations Development Programme and the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights published a participatory review in April 2020 examining the legal, social and human-rights environment for people of diverse sexual orientation and gender identity in Liberia.
tangentialFactors:
The 2012 legislative push and the flier campaign followed an external policy announcement, indicating that international advocacy on LGBT rights has at times been met with a domestic backlash rather than accommodation. A trans visitor arriving during a period of heightened international attention to the issue may encounter a more charged public environment.

Public statements by a head of state defending the criminal law, alongside an active private member's bill in 2024, place official hostility and legislative pressure in the same direction as the statute itself. This differs from jurisdictions where criminal law is dormant but retained on the books.

The 2020 UNDP/OHCHR country review signals sustained international scrutiny of Liberia's treatment of sexual- and gender-minority people, but such reporting does not alter the legal position a visitor faces on the ground.
localsOnly:
Liberian residents live under the same one-year penalty for consensual same-sex conduct, and the 2024 bill would expand it substantially if enacted; the proposals reaching children as young as 10 would apply to residents first and hardest.

Residents have no access to legal gender recognition, so identity documents held by Liberians cannot be brought into line with a person's gender. This affects employment, banking and dealings with the Liberia Refugee Repatriation and Resettlement Commission or other state bodies that require matching documents.

The documented mob violence and the distribution of fliers naming or targeting gay-rights supporters are risks borne primarily by local activists and community members, who have no hate-crime protection sourced in the available material.
outOfScopeNotes:
How often the one-year sodomy penalty is actually prosecuted is unresolved in the available sources; the inventory establishes the statute and the legislative environment, not conviction data.

The fate of the 2024 anti-homosexuality bill after October 2024 is unresolved; the sources do not record a vote, committee action or enactment.

Whether any hate-crime or aggravated-penalty provision explicitly covers gender identity is not sourced here. The inventory addresses sexual-orientation criminalisation and general hostility; trans-specific offences, and any protection against discrimination in services or accommodation, remain not sourced.

Entry, visa and border-screening treatment of trans travellers, including whether passport gender markers are checked against presentation, is not addressed by any source in this inventory.
